Both the news report and the questions will be spoken only once. After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices marked A), B), C) and D). Then mark the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 1 with a single line through the centre.

transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A new study has found that eating nuts regularly can significantly reduce the risk of heart disease and improve overall health, according to researchers at Imperial College London. The study analyzed data from over 800,000 people and found that those who ate at least a handful of nuts per day had a 20 percent lower risk of heart disease and a 25 percent lower risk of dying from heart disease compared to those who rarely or never ate nuts. All types of nuts showed benefits, including almonds, walnuts, peanuts, and pistachios. Researchers say that nuts are rich in healthy fats, protein, fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants, which help reduce inflammation and improve cholesterol levels. They note that while nuts are high in calories, they don't seem to cause weight gain when eaten in moderation, possibly because they make people feel full and satisfied.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the Imperial College London study find about nuts?
2. Why might nuts be good for heart health?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: The city of Barcelona, Spain has introduced an innovative urban planning concept called "superblocks" to reduce traffic, improve air quality, and create more public space for residents. A superblock is a group of nine city blocks where through traffic is restricted, and the streets inside are turned into pedestrian-friendly spaces with parks, playgrounds, and outdoor seating. Cars can still access the superblock to drop off or pick up people or goods, but they can't drive through it. The city says that superblocks reduce traffic congestion and noise, improve air quality, encourage walking and cycling, and create more community space. The program has been controversial—some business owners worry that reduced car access will hurt their businesses, and some residents complain about parking difficulties. But supporters say the benefits to public health and quality of life far outweigh the costs.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What are Barcelona's "superblocks"?
4. What is one benefit of superblocks mentioned in the passage?
5. What is one criticism of the superblock program?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Astronomers have discovered a new Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone of a nearby star, raising the possibility that it could have liquid water and potentially support life. The planet, called TOI-700 d, is located about 100 light-years from Earth and orbits a small, cool star called a red dwarf. It's about the same size as Earth and receives about the same amount of energy from its star as Earth receives from the sun, which means temperatures could be right for liquid water to exist on the surface. The planet was discovered by NASA's TESS satellite, which searches for planets around nearby stars. While more research is needed to determine if the planet has an atmosphere and what it's made of, the discovery is an exciting step in the search for habitable worlds beyond our solar system.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Tom): Hey Sarah, thanks for inviting me skiing this weekend! I'm really excited, but I'm also kind of nervous. I've never been skiing before.
Woman (Sarah): Oh, don't worry! It's going to be fun. Everyone has to start somewhere. I'll help you learn the basics.
Man: Really? You'd do that? That's great. I have no idea what I'm doing. What do I even need to bring?

Woman: Well, first of all, you need warm clothes. It's going to be cold up in the mountains. You'll need a warm jacket, snow pants, gloves, a hat, and goggles. And make sure you wear layers—you'll be cold when you're standing still, but you'll warm up when you're skiing.
Man: Okay, I have most of that. What about equipment? Do I need to buy skis and boots and all that?
Woman: No, you can rent everything at the ski resort. That's what most beginners do. You can rent skis, boots, poles, and even a helmet. You should definitely wear a helmet, by the way—safety first.
Man: Yeah, I'll definitely rent a helmet. I don't want to hurt myself. What about lessons? Should I take a lesson first?

Woman: That's probably a good idea. It's better to learn the basics from a professional instructor than to try to figure it out on your own. They'll teach you how to stop, how to turn, and how to get up when you fall. And you'll progress much faster.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. I'll sign up for a beginner lesson. What are the slopes like? I've heard there are different levels.

Woman: Yeah, there are. Green circles are the easiest—they're for beginners. Blue squares are intermediate, and black diamonds are advanced. We'll start on the green slopes, obviously. Don't worry—they're really gentle.
Man: Good. I'm still kind of nervous about falling. Does it hurt?

Woman: You will fall—everyone falls when they're learning. But as long as you fall correctly and don't hit anything, it usually doesn't hurt too bad. The snow is soft, and you're moving slowly on the beginner slopes.
Man: Okay, that's reassuring. What else should I know?

Woman: Well, make sure you drink plenty of water. It's easy to get dehydrated at high altitude, even in the cold. And don't forget sunscreen—the sun is strong up there, and the snow reflects it. You can get a sunburn even on a cloudy day.
Man: Oh, right! I wouldn't have thought of that. Thanks for the tips.
Woman: No problem! It's going to be fun. And hey, even if you're not very good at it at first, it's still a great way to spend a day outside in the mountains.
Man: Yeah, I'm sure I'll have a good time. Thanks again for inviting me and for all the advice.
Woman: No problem! I'm looking forward to it. Okay, I'll pick you up early Saturday morning, around 6 am. We want to get there when the slopes open.
Man: 6 am? Wow, that's early. But okay, I'll be ready.
Woman: Great! See you then.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
8. Why is Tom nervous about going skiing?
9. What does Sarah say about equipment?
10. What does Sarah recommend for a beginner?
11. What time will Sarah pick Tom up on Saturday?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Hannah): Hey Oliver, I heard you're thinking about studying abroad next year. Have you decided where you want to go?
Man (Oliver): Not yet. I'm trying to decide between Italy, Spain, and France. All three sound amazing, but I don't know which one to choose.
Woman: Oh, that's a tough decision. All three are great countries. What are you most looking for in a study abroad experience?
Man: Well, I want to improve my language skills, of course. But I also want to experience the culture, try new food, travel, and meet new people.
Woman: Yeah, those are all important. Which language are you best at?
Man: I've been studying Spanish for the longest time—since high school. But I've also been studying French for a couple of years, and I just started learning Italian.
Woman: Hmm. Well, if you want to improve your language skills the most, you should probably go to a country where you already have some foundation. That way you can build on what you already know.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. But I've always wanted to go to Italy too. The food, the history, the art... it all sounds amazing.

Woman: Italy is amazing, I've been there. But if you're just starting to learn Italian, it might be harder to keep up with classes if they're taught in Italian. Unless you're taking classes in English, of course.
Man: Yeah, that's a good point. I could take classes in English, but then I wouldn't improve my Italian as much. What about Spain? You studied abroad in Spain, right?

Woman: Yeah, I studied in Madrid for a semester. It was one of the best experiences of my life. The people are so friendly, the food is amazing, and there's so much to see and do. And it's relatively affordable compared to some other European countries.
Man: That's good to hear. What was the hardest part about studying abroad in Spain?

Woman: Well, the first few weeks were hard—getting used to the language, the culture, the food schedule. They eat dinner really late in Spain, like 9 or 10 pm. And everything shuts down in the afternoon for siesta. But once you get used to it, it's great.
Man: Yeah, I've heard about that. What about France? Do you know anyone who studied there?

Woman: My sister studied in Paris. She loved it, but she said it was really expensive. And Parisians have a reputation for being... well, not the friendliest to people who don't speak French well. Though that's probably just a stereotype.
Man: Yeah, I've heard that too. But France has such great art and history and food. It's hard to choose.

Woman: You know what? You should think about what's most important to you. Is it language improvement? Then Spain, since you've studied Spanish the longest. Is it art and history? Maybe Italy or France. Is it affordability? Probably Spain.
Man: Yeah, you're right. I need to figure out my priorities.
Woman: And you could always travel to the other countries during breaks. If you study in Spain, you can easily take a trip to France or Italy on a long weekend. They're not that far apart.
Man: Oh, that's a good point! I didn't think about that. I could travel around Europe while I'm there.
Woman: Definitely! That's one of the best parts of studying abroad in Europe—all the countries are close together, so you can travel a lot.
Man: Hmm, you're making a good case for Spain. Maybe I should go with Spain.
Woman: I think you'd love it! And I can give you all my tips and recommendations for Madrid.
Man: That would be great! Thanks, Hannah. You've been really helpful.
Woman: No problem! I'm excited for you. Studying abroad is such an amazing experience.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of the internet is a story of innovation, collaboration, and rapid change. What began as a small research project in the 1960s has grown into a global network that connects billions of people and has transformed almost every aspect of modern life.

The internet had its origins in the 1960s, when the United States Department of Defense started a research project called ARPANET. The goal was to create a decentralized communication network that could survive a nuclear attack. Instead of going through a central hub, information would travel through multiple paths, so if one part of the network was destroyed, the rest would still work.

In the 1970s and 1980s, the network grew as more universities and research institutions joined. Scientists and researchers used it to share data and communicate with each other. But it was still mostly used by academics and government researchers, not by the general public.

The big change came in the early 1990s, when a British scientist named Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN in Switzerland. The web was different from the internet itself—the internet is the network of computers, while the web is a system of documents and pages that are accessed through the internet. Berners-Lee created the first web browser, the first web server, and the first website. He also developed the basic technologies that the web still uses today: HTML, HTTP, and URLs.

The invention of the web made the internet accessible to everyone, not just computer experts. In the 1990s, the internet grew rapidly as millions of people started using email, browsing websites, and joining online communities. Companies started doing business online, creating the "dot-com" boom.

Since then, the internet has continued to evolve. The 2000s saw the rise of social media, online video, and e-commerce. The 2010s brought mobile internet, cloud computing, and streaming services. And today, the internet is an essential part of daily life for billions of people around the world.

It's hard to imagine what life was like before the internet. It has changed how we communicate, how we work, how we learn, how we shop, how we entertain ourselves, and how we connect with each other. And it continues to evolve and change every day.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Music has been a part of human culture for thousands of years, and scientists are beginning to understand why it has such a powerful effect on us. Research has shown that music doesn't just entertain us—it actually affects our brains and bodies in profound ways, influencing our mood, our memory, our health, and even our ability to learn.

One of the most well-known effects of music is its ability to influence mood. Upbeat, fast music can make us feel energized and happy, while slow, calm music can help us relax and reduce stress. This is because music affects the release of neurotransmitters in the brain, like dopamine (the "feel-good" chemical) and serotonin (which regulates mood). Listening to music you enjoy releases dopamine, giving you pleasure and making you feel good.

Music also has a powerful effect on memory. That's why a song from your past can bring back vivid memories and emotions, even from many years ago. Music activates many different areas of the brain at once, including areas involved in memory, emotion, and movement. This is why music therapy is often used to help people with memory loss, like Alzheimer's patients—music can help them remember things and connect with the world.

Learning to play a musical instrument has even more benefits. It's like a full-body workout for the brain, requiring coordination, memory, concentration, and creativity. Studies have shown that children who learn to play an instrument tend to have better academic performance, better spatial reasoning skills, and improved memory. And learning music as an adult can help keep the brain sharp and may even help prevent cognitive decline as we age.

Music also has physical health benefits. Listening to music can lower blood pressure, reduce heart rate, and decrease stress hormones. It can even reduce pain—studies have shown that music therapy can help reduce pain in patients after surgery or with chronic pain conditions. And singing in a choir has been shown to boost the immune system and improve mental health.

Of course, music is also just enjoyable. It brings people together, it helps us express ourselves, and it enriches our lives in countless ways. But it's fascinating to learn that there's real science behind why music affects us so deeply.
Questions 20 to 22 are based on the passage you have just heard.
20. How does music affect mood?
21. Why is music used to help people with memory loss?
22. What is one benefit of learning to play a musical instrument?

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The global water crisis is one of the most pressing challenges of the 21st century. While water covers about 71 percent of the Earth's surface, only about 2.5 percent of that is fresh water, and most of that is locked up in glaciers and ice caps. That means less than 1 percent of the world's fresh water is easily accessible for human use.

As the world's population grows and the climate changes, more and more people are facing water scarcity. Today, about 2 billion people don't have access to safe drinking water, and more than twice that number don't have access to proper sanitation. By 2050, it's estimated that half of the world's population could be living in areas with water shortages.

Agriculture is the biggest user of fresh water, accounting for about 70 percent of global water use. Growing food requires huge amounts of water—for example, it takes about 1,800 gallons of water to produce just one pound of beef, and about 150 gallons to produce one pound of wheat. As the world's population grows and people eat more meat, the demand for water for agriculture will only increase.

Industry is another major user of water, accounting for about 20 percent of global water use. Factories use water for manufacturing, cooling, and cleaning. And energy production also uses a lot of water—power plants need water to cool their equipment, and producing biofuels requires large amounts of water.

Climate change is making the water crisis worse. Rising temperatures lead to more evaporation and drier soil, which means less water available for drinking, farming, and other uses. Climate change also causes more extreme weather events, like droughts and floods, which can disrupt water supplies.

But there are solutions to the water crisis. Conservation and efficiency are key—using less water and using it more wisely. This includes things like fixing leaky pipes, using more efficient irrigation methods in agriculture, and using water-efficient appliances in homes.

Desalination—turning salt water into fresh water—is another solution, though it's currently expensive and uses a lot of energy. And recycling and reusing wastewater can also help increase water supplies.

Protecting wetlands and watersheds is also important, as these natural ecosystems help filter and clean water and maintain water supplies. And addressing climate change is essential for ensuring that we have enough water in the future.
The global water crisis is a complex problem, but it's not hopeless. With the right policies, technologies, and changes in behavior, we can ensure that everyone has access to clean, safe water.

23. How much of the Earth's water is fresh water?
24. What is the biggest user of fresh water?
25. What is one solution to the water crisis mentioned in the passage?
